short: Rome's most successful love poet was banished for life to the Black Sea coast.
full:
In AD 8, at the height of his fame, Augustus banished the poet Ovid from Rome to Tomis, a Greek colony on the Black Sea in the newly annexed province of Moesia. Ovid himself gave the cause as carmen et error, "a poem and a mistake": the poem was almost certainly his Ars Amatoria, a playful manual of seduction that sat awkwardly beside Augustus's moral legislation on marriage; the error was never named and remains unknown.

Ovid spent the rest of his life at Tomis, petitioning unsuccessfully for recall through the verse letters collected as the Tristia and Epistulae ex Ponto. He died there around AD 17, still in exile under Tiberius. The episode became a byword for the vulnerability of even Rome's most celebrated writers to the emperor's displeasure, and for poetry's capacity to give offence long after publication.
